issues.legal_issue: An assessee’s accounting entries that characterize expenditure as relating to immature plants are an admission but are not conclusive of the expenditure’s actual nature.
material_facts: The assessee had capitalised part of its general expenses and allocated them to the maintenance of immature plants in its accounts.
The assessee asserted that its accounts did not correctly disclose the facts and sought an opportunity to establish the actual nature of the expenditure.
The Tribunal’s order did not make clear that the assessee had been given that opportunity.
issues.conclusion: The accounting entries amounted to an important admission, but the assessee could seek to show that the admission was incorrect.
issues.legal_principle: An admission is an important piece of evidence but is not conclusive, and its maker may show that it is incorrect. Explanation (2) to Section 5 of the Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950 excludes expenditure for the cultivation, upkeep or maintenance of immature plants from which no agricultural income was derived during the previous year; the entries could not by themselves conclusively establish that the expenditure fell within that exclusion. The Court relied on no earlier case for this principle.

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_assessment: An assessee’s expenditure is being considered in an agricultural-income-tax assessment.
predicates.account_books_record_expense_as_immature: The assessee’s account books record expenditure as relating to the cultivation, upkeep, or maintenance of immature plants.

issues.definition: When an assessee’s account books record expenditure as relating to immature plants in an agricultural-income-tax assessment, that accounting admission can be challenged as incorrect.

issues.legal_issue: A refusal to refer questions for the High Court’s opinion is unwarranted when the Tribunal’s order does not establish that the assessee had an opportunity to challenge the factual accuracy of its accounting entries.
material_facts: The assessee sought a reference of questions concerning whether the accounting treatment of expenses precluded their deduction and whether the nature of the expenses should be considered independently of that treatment.
The Tribunal disallowed the expenses, relying on their treatment in the accounts and on its decision for the previous assessment year.
The Tribunal’s order did not make clear that the assessee had been afforded an opportunity to establish that its accounts did not reflect the actual facts.
The High Court declined to direct the Tribunal to refer the questions.
issues.conclusion: The questions arose for consideration, and the High Court should have directed the Tribunal to refer them for its opinion.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 60(2) of the Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, the High Court should direct a reference when the questions arise from the Tribunal’s order. If the Tribunal examines and rejects the assessee’s contention that its accounts do not disclose the real facts, its resulting finding may be one of fact; but where the order does not show that the assessee had a proper opportunity to establish that contention, the questions concerning the accounting treatment and the nature of the expenditure arise for consideration. The Court did not decide whether the earlier High Court decision was correct and relied on no earlier case.

predicates.appeal_challenges_refusal_to_direct_refe: An appeal challenges a refusal to direct a tribunal to refer questions for a High Court’s opinion.
predicates.tribunal_order_unclear_about_opportunity: The tribunal’s order does not establish that the assessee had an opportunity to challenge the accuracy of accounting entries relied on to disallow expenditure.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a refusal to direct a reference and the tribunal’s order does not establish that the assessee could challenge the accounting entries, the High Court must direct the reference.
